```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```
## 1. Conduct a permutation test

Conduct a permutation test to investigate the following question:

> Do homes built pre-1970 have higher average lead soil concentrations?

To perform this test, you'll need the `exide-property-covariates.csv` file found in `/courses/EDS222/data`. This file contains the year each property was built.

::: {.callout-note}

The question is about _average lead soil concentrations_. You'll need to first get the average lead soil concentration for each property, then join your result to the property covariate data to get the year the house was built.



Null hypothesis: There is no difference in lead concentration in homes built pre-1970 and homes built post-1970.

Alternate hypothesis: Houses built pre-1970 have higher levels of lead concentration than those built post-1970.


```{r}
# Reading in data
covariate <- read.csv("data/exide-property-covariates.csv")

soilcores <- read.csv("data/exide-soil-cores (1).csv")
```

```{r}
# Summarizing average lead concentration by property
propconc <- soilcores |> 
    summarise(meanconc = mean(pb_ppm, na.rm= TRUE), .by = property_id)
```

```{r}
# Merging two dfs

everything <- merge(propconc,covariate, by = "property_id")
```

```{r}
# Creating column for pre post 1970 build

everything <- everything |> 
    mutate(before1970 = year_built <1970) 

observedstat <- everything |> 
    summarise(mean = mean(meanconc),.by = before1970)

oldnewdif <- observedstat[1,2] - observedstat[2,2]
```

```{r}
# Visualizing lead concentration in houses by build date

everything |> 
    ggplot(
        aes(x = meanconc, color = before1970)
    )+
        geom_histogram(alpha = 0.1)
```

```{r}
# Sampling one time

samplstat <- everything |> 
    mutate(sampleid = sample(before1970)) |> 
    summarise(mean = mean(meanconc),.by = sampleid) 

sampdif <- samplstat[1,2] - samplstat[2,2]
```

```{r}
# Rerunning sampling 10000 times
permutation <- replicate(n = 10000,
{
   samplstat <- everything |> 
    mutate(sampleid = sample(before1970)) |> 
    summarise(mean = mean(meanconc),.by = sampleid) 

sampdif <- samplstat[1,2] - samplstat[2,2] 
}
)
permutation <- data.frame(permutation)
```

```{r}
# Visualize null distribution

permutation |> 
    ggplot(
        aes(x = permutation)
    )+
        geom_histogram() +
        geom_vline(xintercept = oldnewdif)
```

```{r}
# Calculating p value

mean(permutation >= oldnewdif)
```

The p value is 0. This means that 0 percent of the data from the permutation is greater than our observed difference between lead concentration in pre70s houses and post70s houses.


:::

## 2. Estimate a confidence interval

Estimate a confidence interval to investigate the following question:

> How much is the difference in average lead soil concentrations between properties within 1km of a freeway and those farther away?

```{r}
# Creating observed stat
everything <- everything |> 
    mutate(within1kmfree = (dist_to_freeway_m < 1000)) 

freeway <- everything|> 
    summarise(concbyprox = mean(meanconc), .by = within1kmfree)

sampstatfree <- freeway$concbyprox[1] - freeway$concbyprox[2] 
```

```{r}
# Visualizing lead concentration in houses by proximity to freeway
everything |> 
    ggplot(
        aes(x = meanconc,color = within1kmfree)
    )+geom_histogram(alpha = 0.1)
```



```{r}
# Bootstrapping, which involves selecting random rows to draw new samples

bootstrapgroup <- everything |> 
    slice_sample(replace = TRUE, n = nrow(everything)) |> 
    summarise(mean = mean(meanconc), .by = within1kmfree)

bootstrapstat <- bootstrapgroup$mean[1] - bootstrapgroup$mean[2]
```

```{r}
# Replicating 10000 times
bootstrap<- replicate(n = 10000,
{
    bootstrapgroup <- everything |> 
    slice_sample(replace = TRUE, n = nrow(everything)) |> 
    summarise(mean = mean(meanconc), .by = within1kmfree) |>
    arrange(desc(within1kmfree)) 

bootstrapstat <- bootstrapgroup$mean[1] - bootstrapgroup$mean[2]
})
```

```{r}
# Visualize the bootstrap
bootstrap <- data.frame(bootstrap)
bootstrap |> 
    ggplot(
        aes(x = bootstrap)
    )+ geom_histogram()
```

```{r}
# Calculating 95% conf int
middle95 <- data.frame(quantile(bootstrap$bootstrap,probs=c(.025,.975)))
middle95
```

```{r}
# Visualizing with 95% conf int
bootstrap |> 
    ggplot(
        aes(x = bootstrap)
    )+ geom_histogram()+
        geom_vline(xintercept = middle95[1,1])+
        geom_vline(xintercept = middle95[2,1]) +
        geom_vline(xintercept = sampstatfree, color = 'purple')

```

We would expect to find our estimate for difference in lead concentration between houses within 1km of a freeway and those further within our confidence interval(47.3814201347324-
109.762161483208) 95% of the times we recreate this survey.


## 3. Simulate a negative result

Recall that a p-value is the probability of observing your sample _if_ the null hypothesis is true. Therefore, if you draw a sample from two groups that part of the same population, you should get a p values less than 0.05 only 5% of the time. In other words, a negative result (no actual difference) will yield a significant p-value at the 0.05 threshold in 5% of samples. This is known as the **false positive rate**.

To simulate a negative result, perform the following.

1. Define a normally-distributed population. Pick any mean and standard deviation.
2. Draw a sample of 50 observations from this population. Assign the first 25 to group A and the second 25 to group B.
3. Conduct a permutation test to investigate whether the mean of group A is greater than the mean of group B.
4. Record your p-value.
5. Repeat the simulation 1,000 times.

```{r}
# 1 and 2
pop <- rnorm(1000, mean = 500, sd = 10)
popsamp <- sample(pop,50)
a <- head(popsamp,25)
b <- tail(popsamp,25)
a_b <- mean(a) - mean(b)

```

```{r}
# Visualizing the population our sample came from
pop |> 
    data.frame() |> 
    ggplot(
        aes(x = pop)
    )+ geom_histogram()
```

```{r}
# Visualizing pdf of pop

pop |> 
    data.frame() |> 
    ggplot(
        aes(x = pop)
    )+
        geom_density()

```

```{r}
# Make permutation
perm1 <- replicate(n = 10000, {
perma <- sample(pop,25)
permb <- sample(pop,25)
mean(perma) - mean(permb)
})
mean(perm1 > a_b)
```

```{r}
# Simulate 1000 times
p1000 <- replicate(n = 1000, {
    pop <- rnorm(1000, mean = 500, sd = 10)
popsamp <- sample(pop,50)
a <- head(popsamp,25)
b <- tail(popsamp,25)
a_b <- mean(a) - mean(b)

perm1 <- replicate(n = 10000, {
perma <- sample(pop,25)
permb <- sample(pop,25)
mean(perma) - mean(permb)
})
mean(perm1 > a_b)
})
```

```{r}
# Visualizing our p-values

p1000 <- data.frame(p1000)
p1000 |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = p1000))+
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01)+
    geom_histogram(data = subset(p1000,p1000 <0.05),fill = "blue", binwidth = 0.01) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, color='green')
```

```{r}
# Verifying p
mean(p1000 < 0.05) # Is close to 0.05
sum(p1000 < 0.05) # Is close to 50

```

When you're done, verify that your p-value is less than 0.05 in approximately 5% (50) of your simulations.
